lectures.title: Amendments: procedure under Article 368 and the key Amendment Acts

parts.t: Article 368 and the three methods of amendment
items: **Article 368 (Part XX):** Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution; governs the amendment powers and procedure of the Indian Constitution, balancing flexibility and rigidity.
Creation/alteration of States (Art. 3), creation/abolition of State Legislative Councils (Art. 169), salaries of judges/officials
Passed by each House separately by a majority of the total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting
Special majority, then ratification by the States

**Federal provisions needing ratification (e.g.):** Presidential election, Union/State executive & legislative relations, Supreme Court & High Courts, 7th Schedule Lists, Art. 368 itself, GST Council.
**Federal Ratification List:** requires ratification by simple majority of ≥ 1/2 States (not all States).
**First amendment requiring State ratification:** the **3rd Amendment, 1954** (Entry 33, Concurrent List).
**Trap:** Qualifications, conditions of office, and tenure of the President do NOT require State ratification.
**Initiation:** a Constitution Amendment Bill (Art. 368) can originate in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (either House); it cannot be introduced / originate in State Legislatures.
**Prior Recommendation:** prior recommendation of the President is NOT required (no prior recommendation needed).
**Passing:** passed by each House separately by Special Majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting).
**No Joint Sitting:** each House must pass the Bill independently with special majority; if one House rejects it, the Bill fails completely.
**Ratification:** certain federal provisions require ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures.
**Presidential Assent:** President shall / must give assent (no veto / return power); made mandatory via the **24th Amendment, 1971**.

parts.t: Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights? The early cases
items: Parliament CAN amend Fundamental Rights under Art. 368
Reaffirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution
Reversed earlier view; Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights
**First:** the Supreme Court first held Fundamental Rights amendable in the **Shankari Prasad** case.
**24th Amendment (1971):** affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights; made President's assent compulsory.

parts.t: The First Amendment, 1951 and the Ninth Schedule
items: **First Constitutional Amendment:** 1951 (1st CAA / First Amendment Act 1951).
**What it added:** the 9th Schedule; Arts. 31A & 31B; clause (4) to Art. 15 (Art. 15(4)); it also restricted Art. 19 rights.
**Purpose:** protected agrarian / land reforms from judicial review.
**The 9th Schedule Shield:** Articles 31A, 31B and the 9th Schedule were added to insulate agrarian and land-reform laws from judicial review on Fundamental Rights grounds.
**Why enacted:** largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare / land acquisition measures.
**9th Schedule:** inserted by the First Amendment (1951): Validation of certain Acts/Regulations (Land reforms).
**First Constitutional Amendment related to reservations:** 1st Amendment Act, 1951.
Affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights; made President's assent compulsory
Abolished Privy Purses and privileges of former princely state rulers
**Preamble:** added Socialist, Secular, Integrity to the Preamble.
**Fundamental Duties:** inserted Part IVA (Art. 51A) with 10 Fundamental Duties.
**Other additions:** added DPSPs 39A, 43A; shifted Education to the Concurrent List; added Part XIV-A.
**Advice to President:** the 42nd made Council of Ministers (CoM) advice completely binding.
**Purpose:** nullified emergency-era distortions; restored fundamental safeguards.
**Right to Property:** removed from Fundamental Rights (FRs); now a legal right under Art. 300A.
**Emergency ground:** replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" ("Armed rebellion" inserted).
**Advice to President:** President can return the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration (one opportunity).
**52nd Amendment (1985):** enacted / introduced the Anti-Defection Law; inserted the 10th Schedule (amended Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191).
**First constitutional recognition of political parties:** 1985 (52nd Amendment – 10th Schedule / Anti-defection).
**61st Amendment (1988/89):** reduced / lowered the voting age from 21 years to 18 years (Art. 326); effective 28 March 1989; first exercised in the 1989 General Election.
**69th Amendment (1991):** conferred special status on Delhi as the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi (Art. 239AA).
**73rd Amendment (1992):** constitutional status to Panchayati Raj; added Part IX (Arts. 243–243O, 3-tier system) & 11th Schedule (29 subjects). Enforced: 24 April 1993.
**73rd, other provisions:** ≥ 1/3 reservation for women; SFC (Art. 243I) & SEC (Art. 243K).
**74th Amendment (1992):** constitutional status to Municipalities; added Part IX-A / IXA (Arts. 243P–243ZG) & 12th Schedule (18 subjects). Enforced: 1 June 1993.
**83rd Amendment (2000):** exempted Arunachal Pradesh from reservations for Scheduled Castes in Panchayats.
**84th Amendment (2001):** froze readjustment / allocation of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats (seat allocations) based on the 1971 Census up to the year 2026.
**86th Amendment (2002):** added Art. 21A (Right to Free & Compulsory Education for ages 6–14); modified Art. 45; added Art. 51A(k), the 11th Fundamental Duty, regarding education of children.
**89th Amendment (2003):** bifurcated the National Commission for SCs/STs into NCSC (Art. 338) and NCST (Art. 338A).
**91st Amendment (2003):** capped the Council of Ministers at max 15% of Lok Sabha / Legislative Assembly (House) strength (Arts. 75(1A), 164(1A)); barred defectors from ministerial posts.
**91st, in short:** strengthened anti-defection provisions and limited the council of ministers' size.
**93rd Amendment (2005/06):** provided 27% OBC reservation in educational institutions (Art. 15(5)).
**97th Amendment (2011):** added the right to form Co-operative Societies (Art. 19(1)(c)), DPSP Art. 43B, and Part IX-B (Arts. 243ZH–243ZT; max 21 directors under Art. 243ZJ).
**99th Amendment (2014):** created the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC); struck down / declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2015 for violating judicial independence.
**100th Amendment (2015):** operationalized the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (exchange of 111 Indian and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves).
**101st Amendment (2016):** introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) effective 1 July 2017; created the GST Council (Art. 279A).
**103rd & 104th Amendments (2019):** 10% EWS reservation; ended Anglo-Indian nominations (effective Jan 2020).
**105th Amendment (2021):** restored the power of State Governments and UTs to identify and notify their own SEBCs (Socially and Educationally Backward Classes).
**106th Amendment (2023):** ~1/3rd Women Reservation in Lok Sabha & State Assemblies.

parts.t: Schedules and Parts added by amendments

items: 44th gave President one opportunity to return advice for reconsideration
91st barred defectors from becoming ministers and enforced the 15% ministry ceiling
86th created the fundamental right to elementary education (Art. 21A, 6–14 yrs)
93rd enabled OBC reservation in higher education admissions
Judicial Review / Special provisions for AP; challenged and struck down portions of the amendment
Upheld validity of the Anti-Defection Law; Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review
Upheld the validity of the 10% EWS quota; economic criteria alone can form a valid basis for classification
**Target group of the Janhit Abhiyan judgement:** Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).

corrections.corrected: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022): upheld the validity of the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act (10% EWS quota).
corrections.checked: The case is Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, WP (C) 55 of 2019, decided 7 Nov 2022 (Supreme Court Observer, https://www.scobserver.in/cases/janhit-abhiyan-union-of-india-ews-reservation-case-background/)
